title: Cargo Passport
dek: You want to know what flies
status_reason: The passport for one item exists today, while registration, location tags and whole-vehicle monitoring are concepts, and the evidence on moved items is still partial.

sentences.text: You have a passport to travel. Cargo that travels in space needs one too.
Everything that flies needs evidence about its risks, and fire in microgravity is just one of them.
A Cargo Passport lists the evidence about the risks of the materials in a cargo item, for each environment along its journey.
One example is a shipment from the ISS, in microgravity, to a lunar base, with lower gravity and enclosed spaces.
Whether a test applies to a cargo item depends on more than the atmosphere.
The passport reads the oxygen share and pressure of the vehicle, the place on board (a locker, the airlock, a spot by an air vent, a charging shelf) and whether the item is powered there.
It keeps each part's material and thickness next to the tests that name it, and marks a test that does not name its gravity.
Every cargo item gets a detailed record of its parts and their materials.
The passport carries a link to that record.
The app reads the passport.
SI searches NASA experiments and research for findings on each material.
It weighs them against the conditions at the destination.
You see what the evidence supports, where it shows a risk, and where there is none.

sentences.text: People make the final call.
Suppose every item has a passport and a tag that says where it is.
Then the whole vehicle could be seen at once.
Picking an item would light it up with its checks.
The same rules would run for every item each time the place or the air changes.
The flammability standard NASA-STD-6001B says Test 1 shall evaluate a material in the worst-case atmosphere to which it could be exposed.

The JSC 29353D flammability guidance says hardware designed for use on ISS is acceptable for transport in pressurized areas of vehicles with higher oxygen concentrations, provided it is unpowered and stowed in a locker or validated fire barrier stowage bag, and that unpowered metal boxes are also acceptable.
The same guidance says hardware not meeting these constraints is to be assessed for flammability at the higher oxygen concentration and pressure.

One report says that historically, programs with up to 30 percent oxygen at 10.2 psia have accepted some flammable hardware by material usage agreement, based on the hardware being largely crew-tended while in use and stowed in a nonflammable container when not in use.
The passport would not replace these procedures: it would carry their results with the item and flag when the place or the air no longer matches them.

beats.heading: Same item, new conditions, same questions

sentences.text: The same method can work on Earth too, in planes and submarines.
Four stories from the shelf. Each follows what the experiments tell us and what is still unknown.

limits: The instrument is an illustrative item, not a record.
Registration, tags that report where an item is and whole-vehicle monitoring are concepts, and nothing here says they exist.
Each cited sentence reports what one source says, for the conditions that source names.
A result for one material, thickness, pressure or atmosphere does not stand in for another.
The passport flags evidence and gaps, it gives no verdict, and people decide.

open_questions.text: How does a flame behave at Moon or Mars gravity?
What would an overheating battery do in weightlessness?
How might the air planned for a Moon base change how a fire starts and spreads?
